level1.intro.subject: program
level1.intro.text: You typed {lines} and clicked Run. At this level your program is still just text, as you wrote it. Your computer stores it as [[byte|bytes]], which the next zoom level shows. Highlighted words, like that one, open a short explanation.

level1.size.subject: program
level1.size.text: Your program has {lines} and {characters}, counting the spaces and the invisible [[newline|newline]] at the end of each line.

level2.intro.subject: program
level2.intro.text: A computer can’t store letters as such: it stores [[byte|bytes]], numbers from 0 to 255. So each character of your program becomes a number, or a few numbers, using an agreement called [[utf8|UTF-8]]. Even the spaces at the start of a line, and the ends of lines, are stored.

level2.caption.subject: program
level2.caption.text: Your program in bytes: {bytes}, shown line by line, the same bytes a file of it would hold. Each box shows the byte in hexadecimal, then as an ordinary number. Select one to see its character.

byte.character.subject: byte
byte.character.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.character.text: Every character has an agreed number. **{char}** is {value}. This agreement is called [[utf8|UTF-8]], and for English letters and common symbols, each character takes exactly one [[byte|byte]].

byte.multiByte.subject: byte
byte.multiByte.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {charBytes}
byte.multiByte.text: Every character has an agreed number, but only English letters and common symbols fit in one [[byte|byte]]. [[utf8|UTF-8]] stores **{char}** as {charSize}: **{charBytes}**. This byte is the {placeInChar} of them.

byte.newline.subject: byte
byte.newline.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.newline.text: The [[newline|newline]] at the end of line {line}. You can’t see it, but it is stored as number **{value}**, and it tells Python the line is over.

byte.indent.subject: byte
byte.indent.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.indent.text: One of the {indent} that indent line {line}. Indentation is stored like any other character, as number **{value}**, and for Python it matters: it says which lines belong together.

byte.indentOneSpace.subject: byte
byte.indentOneSpace.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.indentOneSpace.text: The space that indents line {line}. Indentation is stored like any other character, as number **{value}**, and for Python it matters: it says which lines belong together.

byte.quote.subject: byte
byte.quote.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.quote.text: A quote mark is stored like any other character. Python uses the pair of them to find where a piece of text starts and ends.

byte.bits.subject: byte
byte.bits.title: How the number {value} is stored
byte.bits.text: A byte is 8 [[bit|bits]]: 8 tiny on/off switches. Each switch has a value, shown under it. Add up the values of the switches that are on, and you get the number. This way of counting is called [[binary|binary]].

byte.bitsPattern.subject: byte
byte.bitsPattern.text: So **{char}** is stored as the pattern **{bits}**.

byte.bitsPatternMultiByte.subject: byte
byte.bitsPatternMultiByte.text: So the {placeInChar} byte of **{char}** is stored as the pattern **{bits}**.

level3.intro.subject: program
level3.intro.text: To understand code, Python first needs its words, just as you read words rather than single letters. So it [[encoding|decodes]] your {bytes} into text and picks out the meaningful pieces, called [[token|tokens]]. In Python, indentation matters, so the tokens also mark where an indented block starts and ends.

level3.caption.subject: program
level3.caption.text: Your program, line by line, as the {tokens} Python found. Select one to see what it is.

level3.encoding.subject: program
level3.encoding.text: **ENCODING** comes before line 1: Python’s note that it read your bytes as **{encoding}**. It isn’t part of your code.

token.name.subject: token
token.name.title: **{text}** is a name
token.name.text: Python has read the letters of **{text}** and decided they form one word: a **name**. It doesn’t know yet what the name means.

token.keyword.subject: token
token.keyword.title: **{text}** is a keyword
token.keyword.text: **{text}** is a keyword: a name reserved by Python, which you can’t use for your own things. The tokenizer still calls it a **NAME**; working out that it’s special comes next.

token.openBracket.subject: token
token.openBracket.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.openBracket.text: An opening bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.closeBracket.subject: token
token.closeBracket.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.closeBracket.text: A closing bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.openSquare.subject: token
token.openSquare.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.openSquare.text: An opening square bracket. It starts a list, as in [1, 2], or picks something out, as in names[0]. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.closeSquare.subject: token
token.closeSquare.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.closeSquare.text: A closing square bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.colon.subject: token
token.colon.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.colon.text: A colon. After if, for, def and the like, it says the block they control comes next. Colons have other jobs too, as in dictionaries and slices. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.comma.subject: token
token.comma.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.comma.text: A comma: it separates things, such as the items of a list, or what a function is given. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.equals.subject: token
token.equals.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.equals.text: An equals sign. In a line like x = 1, the name on its left gets the value on its right. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.op.subject: token
token.op.title: **{text}** is punctuation or an operator
token.op.text: The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation, and every operator such as + or ==, **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.number.subject: token
token.number.title: **{text}** is a number
token.number.text: Python has read **{text}** and decided it is one number. Working out its value comes later.

token.string.subject: token
token.string.title: **{text}** is one piece of text
token.string.text: The whole text is one token, quote marks included. Python saw the opening quote mark and kept reading until the closing one.

token.comment.subject: token
token.comment.title: A comment
token.comment.text: Everything from **#** to the end of the line is a comment, written for people. The tokenizer keeps it as a token, but Python ignores it from here on.

token.newline.subject: token
token.newline.title: End of line {line}
token.newline.text: This token comes from byte 10, the invisible [[newline|newline]]. It tells Python the line of code is complete.

token.noCode.subject: token
token.noCode.title: A line with no code
token.noCode.text: Line {line} has no code on it. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but no line of code. Python ignores it from here on.

token.commentLine.subject: token
token.commentLine.title: End of a comment line
token.commentLine.text: Line {line} holds only a comment. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but no line of code. Python ignores it from here on.

token.insideBrackets.subject: token
token.insideBrackets.title: A line break inside brackets
token.insideBrackets.text: Line {line} ends inside brackets, so the line of code goes on to the next line. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE, and Python ignores it from here on.

token.indent.subject: token
token.indent.title: A block starts
token.indent.text: Line {line} starts with {indent}, deeper than the line of code before it, so a block starts here. In Python, indentation is part of the meaning.

token.dedent.subject: token
token.dedent.title: A block ends
token.dedent.text: An empty token: line {line} starts further left, at column {column}, so an indented block has ended. Each block that ends gets its own DEDENT.

token.dedentAtEnd.subject: token
token.dedentAtEnd.title: A block ends
token.dedentAtEnd.text: An empty token: line {line} doesn’t exist, the file has ended, so an indented block has ended. Each block that ends gets its own DEDENT.

token.endmarker.subject: token
token.endmarker.title: End of the file
token.endmarker.text: An empty token with no characters at all. Python adds it when the file runs out, so it knows it has seen everything.

token.other.subject: token
token.other.title: A token tokenize calls {type}
token.other.text: The tokenizer calls this piece of your code a **{type}**.

token.whereLines.subject: token
token.whereLines.text: **Where:** from line {line} to line {endLine}. tokenize writes this as **{position}**.

level4.intro.subject: program
level4.intro.text: Words alone don’t say what goes with what. So Python works out the [[structure|structure]]: which pieces belong together, which lines belong inside which block, and what each line does, recorded as boxes inside boxes.

level4.caption.subject: program
level4.caption.text: Your program as the {boxes} Python made, each inside the box that holds it. Select one to see its role.

level4.noTree.subject: program
level4.noTree.text: Python couldn’t work out the structure of your program, because it has a syntax error. The Terminal shows where.

level4.signposts.subject: program
level4.signposts.title: Where did the brackets, colons and indentation go?
level4.signposts.text: They were signposts. Brackets showed which pieces go together, and colons and indentation showed which lines belong inside a block. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.signpostsBrackets.subject: program
level4.signpostsBrackets.title: Where did the brackets go?
level4.signpostsBrackets.text: They were signposts, showing which pieces go together. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.signpostsBlocks.subject: program
level4.signpostsBlocks.title: Where did the colons and indentation go?
level4.signpostsBlocks.text: They were signposts. Colons and indentation showed which lines belong inside a block. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.notDrawn.subject: node
level4.notDrawn.text: Not drawn: the {inside} inside this one. Your program’s tree is too deep to draw in full.

node.module.subject: node
node.module.title: Your program
node.module.text: The biggest box is the whole program. It holds a list of your program’s statements, {statements} in all. Python calls this box a **Module**.

node.functionDef.subject: node
node.functionDef.title: Define a function
node.functionDef.text: Everything from **def** to the end of its indented block. It has a name, **{name}**, a list of what it takes, and its own list of statements, {statements} in all. Defining it doesn’t run it. Python calls this box a **FunctionDef**.

node.arguments.subject: node
node.arguments.title: What it takes
node.arguments.text: The list of what {function} takes. Python calls this box **arguments**. It doesn’t match any single piece of your code.

node.argOnly.subject: node
node.argOnly.title: One input
node.argOnly.text: The one input {function} takes: **{name}**. When {function} is called, whatever it is given gets this name, inside {function} only. Python calls this an **arg**.

node.arg.subject: node
node.arg.title: One input
node.arg.text: One of the inputs {function} takes: **{name}**. When {function} is called, what it is given for this input gets this name, inside {function} only. Python calls this an **arg**.

node.expr.subject: node
node.expr.title: One statement
node.expr.text: A statement that does something and doesn’t keep the answer, which is fine: nobody needs it. Python calls it an **Expr** statement.

node.call.subject: node
node.call.title: Call a function
node.call.text: A call has two parts: what to call, and what to give it. This one calls **{func}**. Python calls this box a **Call**.

node.name.subject: node
node.name.title: A name
node.name.text: Just a name for now: **{name}**. Python doesn’t know yet what it points to. It looks the name up when the program runs. Python calls this a **Name**.

node.nameStore.subject: node
node.nameStore.title: A name
node.nameStore.text: The name **{name}** is given a value here. Python calls this a **Name** being stored.

node.nameStoreLoop.subject: node
node.nameStoreLoop.title: A name
node.nameStoreLoop.text: The name **{name}** is given a value each trip round the loop. Python calls this a **Name** being stored.

node.constantText.subject: node
node.constantText.title: A fixed value
node.constantText.text: A fixed value typed straight into your code: **{value}**. The quote marks are gone; they only marked where the text starts and ends. Python calls this a **Constant**.

node.constant.subject: node
node.constant.title: A fixed value
node.constant.text: A fixed value typed straight into your code: **{value}**. Python calls this a **Constant**.

node.for.subject: node
node.for.title: A loop
node.for.text: Everything from **for** to the end of its indented block. It has a name each item gets (**{target}**), something to go through (**{iter}**) and what to do each time ({statements}). Python calls this box a **For**.

node.list.subject: node
node.list.title: A list
node.list.text: The list **{code}**, with its {items}. Python calls this box a **List**.

node.assign.subject: node
node.assign.title: Store a value
node.assign.text: Python works out the value on the right of the **=**, then stores it in **{target}**, on the left. Python calls this box an **Assign**.

node.binOp.subject: node
node.binOp.title: A calculation
node.binOp.text: Two values with an operator between them, **{operator}**. Python works out the answer when the program runs. Python calls this box a **BinOp**, short for “binary operation”: an operation on two values. It calls the operator **{op}**.

node.if.subject: node
node.if.title: A choice
node.if.text: It has a test, **{test}**. If the test is true, Python runs the {statements} indented under it. If not, it moves on to the **elif** or **else** part, if there is one. Python calls this box an **If**.

node.return.subject: node
node.return.title: Hand back an answer
node.return.text: It ends the function and hands an answer back to whoever called it: what comes after **return**, or None if nothing does. Python calls this box a **Return**.

node.attribute.subject: node
node.attribute.title: A part of something
node.attribute.text: The dot reaches inside **{owner}** for something it has, called **{name}**. Python calls this an **Attribute**.

node.other.subject: node
node.other.title: Part of your program
node.other.text: Python calls this box a **{type}**. It stands for this part of your code: **{code}**.

node.otherNoPlace.subject: node
node.otherNoPlace.title: Part of the structure
node.otherNoPlace.text: Python calls this box a **{type}**. It doesn’t match any single piece of your code.

field.call.keywords.subject: node
field.call.keywords.text: what to give it, by name

terminal.cutShort.subject: program
terminal.cutShort.text: Your program ran too long to record in full. The app records up to 2,000 steps of a run, so the record of yours stops partway. Everything it printed is above.

tryIt.observed.subject: program
tryIt.observed.text: Your browser’s Python did what this command does, on your program, just now.

tryIt.nothingPrinted.subject: program
tryIt.nothingPrinted.text: Nothing: your program doesn’t print anything, so the terminal shows nothing either.

tryIt.level1.printed.subject: program
tryIt.level1.printed.text: Each line here is a line your program printed, in order.

tryIt.level1.error.subject: program
tryIt.level1.error.text: Your program stopped with an error. The last line names the error and says what went wrong; the lines above it say where. The path is where your browser’s Python saved {file}. On your computer, you’ll see your own folder.

tryIt.level2.multiByte.subject: byte
tryIt.level2.multiByte.text: Numbers from 128 to 255 come in groups of 2 to 4. [[utf8|UTF-8]] stores each character beyond English letters and common symbols that way: **{char}** is {charBytes}.

tryIt.level3.tokens.subject: program
tryIt.level3.tokens.text: After ENCODING, each line is one of the tokens at this zoom level, in the same order.

tryIt.tokenRow.encoding.subject: program
tryIt.tokenRow.encoding.text: Not a place in your file: Python’s note of the [[encoding|encoding]] it read your bytes with.

tryIt.tokenRow.position.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.position.text: Line {line}, {columns}. In each pair, the first number is the line and the second is the column. The end is the first column after the token. Columns count from 0.

tryIt.tokenRow.newline.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.newline.text: The end of a complete line of code.

tryIt.tokenRow.indent.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.indent.text: The {indent} at the start of line {line}: a block starts here.

tryIt.tokenRow.nl.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.nl.text: Line {line}’s newline is an NL, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but not a line of code.

tryIt.tokenRow.dedent.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.dedent.text: An empty token: a block has ended, because line {line} starts further left.

tryIt.tokenRow.dedentAtEnd.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.dedentAtEnd.text: An empty token: a block has ended, because the file has.

tryIt.tokenRow.endmarker.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.endmarker.text: The file has ended, so the token is empty.

tryIt.level4.boxes.subject: program
tryIt.level4.boxes.text: Each name followed by brackets, such as **Call(…)**, is one of the boxes at this zoom level, in the same order. The exceptions are **Load()**, **Store()** and **Del()**, and operators such as **Add()** or **Lt()**: each says what the box around it does.

tryIt.level4.indent.subject: program
tryIt.level4.indent.text: The indentation shows which box sits inside which.

tryIt.astRow.module.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.module.text: Your program. **body** is its list of statements: here, {statements}.

tryIt.astRow.functionDef.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.functionDef.text: The function: its name, what it takes, and its own list of statements.

tryIt.astRow.for.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.for.text: The loop: **target** is the name each item gets, **iter** is what to go through, **body** is what to do each time.

tryIt.astRow.expr.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.expr.text: One statement. **value** is what it does.

tryIt.astRow.call.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.call.text: A call: **func** is what to call, and **args** is what to give it.

tryIt.astRow.nameLoad.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.nameLoad.text: A name: **id** is the name itself. **ctx=Load()** means the name is read.

tryIt.astRow.nameStore.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.nameStore.text: A name being stored: **ctx=Store()** means the name is given a value.

tryIt.astRow.constant.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.constant.text: A fixed value: **value** is the value, as Python writes it.

level5.intro.subject: program
level5.intro.text: Boxes describe meaning, but they aren’t something a computer can carry out step by step. So Python compiles them into lists of simple steps, called [[code|bytecode]]: {lists}. By default, CPython runs your program by reading these steps one at a time, rather than compiling it to your CPU’s own machine code. Then it runs the steps, and some run more than once.

level5.caption.subject: program
level5.caption.text: Your program has {steps}, and {ran} happened, in the order the strip shows. Select a step, or step through with Next.

level5.noBytecode.subject: program
level5.noBytecode.text: Python made no steps from your program, because it has a syntax error. The Terminal shows where.

level5.cutShort.subject: program
level5.cutShort.text: Your program ran more than 2,000 steps, so only the first 2,000 are here.

level5.strip.subject: program
level5.strip.title: Every step that ran, in order
level5.strip.text: Squares are your program’s own steps; circles are the steps of the code inside it, such as a function. Filled ones have run.

level5.plates.subject: program
level5.plates.title: Plates, after this step
level5.plates.text: What Python is holding in each [[frame|frame]], on its [[stack|plates]], and each frame’s variables.

level5.platesUnsure.subject: program
level5.platesUnsure.text: Python’s rules can’t account for this frame’s plates from here, so they aren’t shown.

level5.noFrames.subject: program
level5.noFrames.text: No frames: your program has finished.

level5.objects.subject: program
level5.objects.title: Objects, so far
level5.objects.text: The [[heap|objects]] the plates and variables have pointed to so far. Those still in use after this step are outlined. Each of Python’s own types gives its size in bytes, as Python in your browser measures it; Python on a 64-bit computer uses more bytes for the same object. A list or dictionary is shown as it was when last seen.

level5.recipe.subject: step
level5.recipe.title: {code}’s recipe card
level5.recipe.text: What the compiler wrote down with the steps: the names they use, their fixed values, and their own variables.

level5.note.subject: program
level5.note.text: Next and Back follow the order the steps ran in, moving between your program and the code inside it. The steps, the order they ran in and the recipe cards are observed from your program. The plates and objects are derived: worked out from what each step does, using Python’s rules, because Python can’t show them directly.

level6.intro.subject: program
level6.intro.text: Here the zoom stops following your code and starts showing the program that reads it. By default, CPython never compiles your code to CPU instructions. It keeps your steps as bytecode, and its [[py|interpreter]], a program written in [[clang|C]] and compiled long before you ran anything, reads them one at a time and runs a piece of its own C code for each. Python 3.13 and later also come with an experimental JIT compiler that can turn busy steps into machine code, but it is off unless you switch it on.

level6.yourProgram.subject: program
level6.yourProgram.title: Your program
level6.yourProgram.text: {file} → tokens → structure → bytecode. Translated as far as bytecode, then followed step by step.

level6.pythonItself.subject: program
level6.pythonItself.title: Python itself
level6.pythonItself.text: C source → machine code → CPU. Translated long before you ran anything: to machine code, or in your browser, to WebAssembly.

level6.loop.subject: program
level6.loop.text: The interpreter repeats the same 4 moves for every step.

level6.read.subject: step
level6.read.text: **1 · Read** the next step: step {number} of {code}.

level6.lookUp.subject: step
level6.lookUp.text: **2 · Look up** the C code for it: {handlers}.

level6.lookUpTypical.subject: step
level6.lookUpTypical.text: **2 · Look up** the C code for it: {opname}, or the faster form Python rewrote it into.

level6.run.subject: program
level6.run.text: **3 · Run** that C code, shown below.

level6.moveOn.subject: program
level6.moveOn.text: **4 · Move on** to the next step that runs.

level6.moveOnDone.subject: program
level6.moveOnDone.text: **4 · Move on**: no steps are left, so your program has finished.

level6.runNeverRan.subject: program
level6.runNeverRan.text: **3 · Run** that C code. This step never got that far: it never ran.

level6.step.subject: step
level6.step.title: How the interpreter does step {number} of {code}
level6.step.text: Each sentence matches the real line of [[clang|C]] under it, copied from CPython’s source. If this step ran more than once, pick another run: a busy step can run different C code the second time.

level6.stepTypical.subject: step
level6.stepTypical.title: How the interpreter does step {number} of {code}
level6.stepTypical.text: To run a step like this one, the interpreter looks up its handler: the piece of its own C code for {opname}, which does what the step says. So far this zoom level has the real C code only for two Examples, hello world and greet.py, whose handlers we recorded on every step run. For your program, this is how it usually works.

level6.afterRun.subject: step
level6.afterRun.text: When your program ran without being watched, Python had rewritten this step into **{afterRun}**, a faster form, by the time it finished. A run of the step after the rewrite starts with {afterRun}’s C code.

level6.twice.subject: step
level6.twice.text: On this run the step ran twice over: first in its general form, {general}, which rewrote the step into the faster {faster}, and then in that new form.

level6.ranInside.subject: step
level6.ranInside.text: **No handler of its own ran for this step.** By this run, Python had rewritten it into {handlers}. When Python was built, the compiler copied {handlers}’s code onto the end of {inside}, the handler of the step before, so this check ran there. The [[debugger|debugger]] recorded {handlers}’s code running inside {inside}.

level6.neverRan.subject: step
level6.neverRan.text: This step never ran for your program. Here is the C code of its general form, {opname}, anyway.

level6.recorded.subject: step
level6.recorded.text: Which handlers ran, on each step run, was recorded with a [[debugger|debugger]] on our test machine, running {example} with CPython 3.14.2 on Linux (x86-64), compiled to machine code. In your browser, Python is the same C code compiled to WebAssembly, and the run this page recorded was watched, which stops Python rewriting steps. The C is the same for every Python program that runs these handlers.

level6.license.subject: program
level6.license.text: The C code is quoted from CPython: Copyright (c) 2001 Python Software Foundation; All Rights Reserved. It is used under the PSF License.

step.put.subject: step
step.put.text: This time it put {object} on a plate.

step.printed.subject: step
step.printed.text: {callee} wrote a line to the terminal: {printed}

step.startsFrame.subject: step
step.startsFrame.text: Because {callee} is written in Python, Python doesn’t leave the interpreter to run it: it sets up a fresh [[frame|frame]] for {callee}, with its own plates and variables, and carries on with its steps.

step.neverRan.subject: step
step.neverRan.text: This step **never ran** for your program.

step.afterRun.subject: step
step.afterRun.text: When your program ran again without being watched, Python rewrote this step into **{afterRun}**, a faster form for the objects it met. Watching every step, as this zoom level does, stops Python rewriting them.

step.resume.subject: step
step.resume.title: Get ready
step.resume.text: Every piece of code starts with this step. Python checks whether anything urgent is waiting, such as you pressing Ctrl+C. You didn’t write it; Python adds it.

step.loadConst.subject: step
step.loadConst.title: Get {value}
step.loadConst.text: Python takes the fixed value **{value}** from {code}’s recipe card and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.loadConstCode.subject: step
step.loadConstCode.title: Get {name}’s steps
step.loadConstCode.text: The steps of **{name}** were compiled into a code object of their own. This step puts a label for it on a plate, ready to make a function or a class from it.

step.loadSmallInt.subject: step
step.loadSmallInt.title: Get {value}
step.loadSmallInt.text: Python puts a label for the small number **{value}** on a plate. Python makes the small numbers once, when it starts, so this step needs no fixed value.

step.loadName.subject: step
step.loadName.title: Find {name}
step.loadName.text: Python looks up the name **{name}**: first in the names {code} has so far, then in Python’s built-in toolbox. It puts a label for what it finds on a plate.

step.storeName.subject: step
step.storeName.title: Call it {name}
step.storeName.text: Python takes the label off the top plate and stores it under the name **{name}**, so later steps can find it.

step.loadGlobal.subject: step
step.loadGlobal.title: Find {name}
step.loadGlobal.text: **{name}** isn’t one of {code}’s own variables, so Python looks in your program’s names, then in its built-in toolbox. It puts a label for what it finds on a plate.

step.loadGlobalNull.subject: step
step.loadGlobalNull.title: Find {name}, plus an empty plate
step.loadGlobalNull.text: **{name}** isn’t one of {code}’s own variables, so Python looks in your program’s names, then in its built-in toolbox. It puts a label for what it finds on a plate, then an empty plate, ready for a call.

step.storeGlobal.subject: step
step.storeGlobal.title: Call it {name}, in your program’s names
step.storeGlobal.text: Python takes the label off the top plate and stores it under **{name}** in your program’s names, not in {code}’s own variables.

step.loadFast.subject: step
step.loadFast.title: Get {name}
step.loadFast.text: Python gets {code}’s own variable **{name}** and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.loadFastBorrow.subject: step
step.loadFastBorrow.title: Get {name}
step.loadFastBorrow.text: Python gets {code}’s own variable **{name}** and puts a label for it on a plate. It borrows the label rather than making a new one, which is quicker.

step.loadFastCheck.subject: step
step.loadFastCheck.title: Get {name}
step.loadFastCheck.text: Python gets {code}’s own variable **{name}** and puts a label for it on a plate, after checking that it has been given a value.

step.loadFastLoadFast.subject: step
step.loadFastLoadFast.title: Get {name}
step.loadFastLoadFast.text: Python gets two of {code}’s own variables, **{name}**, in one step, and puts a label for each on a plate.

step.loadFastBorrowLoadFastBorrow.subject: step
step.loadFastBorrowLoadFastBorrow.title: Get {name}
step.loadFastBorrowLoadFastBorrow.text: Python gets two of {code}’s own variables, **{name}**, in one step, and puts a label for each on a plate. It borrows the labels, which is quicker.

step.loadFastAndClear.subject: step
step.loadFastAndClear.title: Put {name} aside
step.loadFastAndClear.text: Python moves the variable **{name}** onto a plate, so the comprehension can use the name for itself. It puts it back afterwards.

step.storeFast.subject: step
step.storeFast.title: Call it {name}
step.storeFast.text: Python takes the label off the top plate and stores it in {code}’s own variable **{name}**.

step.storeFastStoreFast.subject: step
step.storeFastStoreFast.title: Store {name}
step.storeFastStoreFast.text: Python takes two labels off the plates and stores them in two of {code}’s own variables, **{name}**, in one step.

step.storeFastLoadFast.subject: step
step.storeFastLoadFast.title: Store, then get: {name}
step.storeFastLoadFast.text: Python stores the top plate’s label in one of {code}’s own variables, then gets a variable, in one step: **{name}**.

step.loadDeref.subject: step
step.loadDeref.title: Get {name}
step.loadDeref.text: Python gets the variable **{name}**, which {code} shares with the code around it, and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.storeDeref.subject: step
step.storeDeref.title: Call it {name}
step.storeDeref.text: Python takes the label off the top plate and stores it in **{name}**, a variable {code} shares with the code around it.

step.deleteName.subject: step
step.deleteName.title: Forget {name}
step.deleteName.text: Python removes the name **{name}**, so later steps can no longer find it.

step.loadAttr.subject: step
step.loadAttr.title: Get its {name}
step.loadAttr.text: Python takes the object off the top plate, looks up its attribute **{name}**, and puts a label for what it finds on a plate.

step.loadAttrMethod.subject: step
step.loadAttrMethod.title: Find its {name}, ready for a call
step.loadAttrMethod.text: Python takes the object off the top plate and looks up **{name}** on it, ready for a call. For a method, it puts the method on a plate, then the object it belongs to; for anything else, what it found, then an empty plate.

step.storeAttr.subject: step
step.storeAttr.title: Set its {name}
step.storeAttr.text: Python takes two labels off the plates: an object, and a value to store in its attribute **{name}**.

step.pushNull.subject: step
step.pushNull.title: Add an empty plate
step.pushNull.text: An empty plate, ready for a call. When you call a method, such as **name.upper()**, this place holds the object. For a plain function, it stays empty.

step.call.subject: step
step.call.title: Call it with {count}
step.call.text: Python calls the function on the plates. It takes the plates the call needs off, and puts the answer on a plate when the call ends.

step.callNamed.subject: step
step.callNamed.title: Call {callee} with {count}
step.callNamed.text: Python calls **{callee}**. It takes the plates the call needs off: the function, an empty plate or the object it belongs to, and what the call is given. When the call ends, it puts the answer on a plate.

step.callKw.subject: step
step.callKw.title: Call it, with names
step.callKw.text: Python calls a function with things given by name, such as **end=""**. It takes the plates the call needs off, and puts the answer on a plate when the call ends.

step.callFunctionEx.subject: step
step.callFunctionEx.title: Call it with a list of things
step.callFunctionEx.text: Python calls a function with things unpacked from a list or a dictionary, as one or two stars in front of them ask. It puts the answer on a plate when the call ends.

step.popTop.subject: step
step.popTop.title: Throw away the answer
step.popTop.text: Nobody needs what is on the top plate, so Python takes the plate off.

step.returnValue.subject: step
step.returnValue.title: Hand back the answer
step.returnValue.text: {code} has finished. Python takes the label off the top plate and hands it back to whoever ran {code}, then clears away its [[frame|frame]].

step.returnValueProgram.subject: step
step.returnValueProgram.title: Hand back the answer
step.returnValueProgram.text: Python hands the label on the top plate back to whoever started your program, and clears away its [[frame|frame]]. **Your program is finished.**

step.makeFunction.subject: step
step.makeFunction.title: Make a function
step.makeFunction.text: Python takes the code object off the top plate and wraps it into a function object: its steps, plus the names it should use. Now it can be called.

step.loadBuildClass.subject: step
step.loadBuildClass.title: Get the class builder
step.loadBuildClass.text: Python puts a label for its built-in class builder on a plate, ready to make a class.

step.getIter.subject: step
step.getIter.title: Start walking through it
step.getIter.text: To go through the object on the top plate one item at a time, Python asks it for a small helper that remembers how far it has got: a walker, called an **iterator**.

step.forIter.subject: step
step.forIter.title: Take the next item, or stop
step.forIter.text: Python asks the walker for the next item, and puts it on a plate, above the walker. When there are no items left, the loop ends.

step.forIterTrip.subject: step
step.forIterTrip.title: Take the next item, or stop
step.forIterTrip.text: **Trip {trip} round the loop.** Python asks the walker for the next item, and puts it on a plate, above the walker.

step.forIterDone.subject: step
step.forIterDone.title: Take the next item, or stop
step.forIterDone.text: **Trip {trip} round the loop.** The walker has no items left, so the loop ends: Python jumps out of it, to step {next}.

step.endFor.subject: step
step.endFor.title: End of the loop
step.endFor.text: Python takes the last item off the plates when a loop ends the long way round. Usually this step never runs: when the walker runs out, Python jumps straight past it.

step.popIter.subject: step
step.popIter.title: Put the walker away
step.popIter.text: The loop is over. Python takes the walker off its plate and lets it go.

step.jumpBackward.subject: step
step.jumpBackward.title: Back to the top of the loop
step.jumpBackward.text: The end of the loop’s body: Python goes back to step {target} to go round again.

step.jumpForward.subject: step
step.jumpForward.title: Jump ahead to step {target}
step.jumpForward.text: Python skips the steps in between and carries on at step {target}.

step.popJumpIfFalse.subject: step
step.popJumpIfFalse.title: If not, jump to step {target}
step.popJumpIfFalse.text: Python takes the answer off the top plate. If it is false, Python jumps to step {target}; if it is true, it carries on with the next step.

step.popJumpIfTrue.subject: step
step.popJumpIfTrue.title: If so, jump to step {target}
step.popJumpIfTrue.text: Python takes the answer off the top plate. If it is true, Python jumps to step {target}; if it is false, it carries on with the next step.

step.popJumpIfNone.subject: step
step.popJumpIfNone.title: If it is None, jump to step {target}
step.popJumpIfNone.text: Python takes the top plate off. If its label points to [[none|None]], Python jumps to step {target}; otherwise it carries on with the next step.

step.popJumpIfNotNone.subject: step
step.popJumpIfNotNone.title: If it isn’t None, jump to step {target}
step.popJumpIfNotNone.text: Python takes the top plate off. Unless its label points to [[none|None]], Python jumps to step {target}; otherwise it carries on with the next step.

step.notTaken.subject: step
step.notTaken.title: Didn’t jump
step.notTaken.text: A step that does nothing. It marks where the program goes when the jump before it isn’t taken, for tools that follow which way a program went.

step.toBool.subject: step
step.toBool.title: Is it true?
step.toBool.text: Python turns the object on the top plate into True or False, ready for a decision.

step.compareOp.subject: step
step.compareOp.title: Compare with {operator}
step.compareOp.text: Python takes the two top plates off, compares their objects with **{operator}**, and puts the answer, True or False, on a plate.

step.binaryOp.subject: step
step.binaryOp.title: Work out {operator}
step.binaryOp.text: Python takes the two top plates off, works out **{operator}** with their objects, and puts a label for the answer on a plate.

step.binaryOpSubscript.subject: step
step.binaryOpSubscript.title: Look up an item
step.binaryOpSubscript.text: Python takes the two top plates off: an object, and a position or key. It looks up that item in the object, and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.storeSubscr.subject: step
step.storeSubscr.title: Store an item
step.storeSubscr.text: Python takes three plates off: a value, an object, and a position or key. It stores the value in the object, at that position or key.

step.unaryNegative.subject: step
step.unaryNegative.title: Make it negative
step.unaryNegative.text: Python takes the number off the top plate and puts its negative on a plate.

step.unaryNot.subject: step
step.unaryNot.title: Not
step.unaryNot.text: Python takes the top plate off and puts the opposite, True or False, on a plate.

step.isOp.subject: step
step.isOp.title: Is it the same object?
step.isOp.text: Python takes the two top plates off and checks whether their labels point to the same object. It puts the answer, True or False, on a plate.

step.containsOp.subject: step
step.containsOp.title: Is it in there?
step.containsOp.text: Python takes the two top plates off and checks whether the first object is in the second. It puts the answer, True or False, on a plate.

step.buildList.subject: step
step.buildList.title: Make a list of {count}
step.buildList.text: Python takes the {count} off the plates, makes a new list of them, and puts a label for the list on a plate.

step.buildTuple.subject: step
step.buildTuple.title: Make a tuple of {count}
step.buildTuple.text: Python takes the {count} off the plates, makes a tuple of them, a list that can’t change, and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.buildMap.subject: step
step.buildMap.title: Make a dictionary
step.buildMap.text: Python takes the keys and values off the plates, makes a new dictionary of them, and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.buildSet.subject: step
step.buildSet.title: Make a set of {count}
step.buildSet.text: Python takes the {count} off the plates, makes a new set of them, and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.buildString.subject: step
step.buildString.title: Join {count} into text
step.buildString.text: Python takes {count} of text off the plates and joins them into one piece of text, as an f-string asks.

step.formatSimple.subject: step
step.formatSimple.title: Turn it into text
step.formatSimple.text: Python takes the object off the top plate and puts the text that shows it on a plate, for an f-string.

step.formatWithSpec.subject: step
step.formatWithSpec.title: Turn it into text, as asked
step.formatWithSpec.text: Python takes an object and a format, such as **.2f**, off the plates, and puts the text that shows the object in that format on a plate.

step.convertValue.subject: step
step.convertValue.title: Show it with str or repr
step.convertValue.text: Python turns the object on the top plate into text, as **!r**, **!s** or **!a** in an f-string asks.

step.listAppend.subject: step
step.listAppend.title: Add it to the list
step.listAppend.text: Python takes the top plate off and adds its object to the list further down the plates, as a list comprehension does for each item.

step.listExtend.subject: step
step.listExtend.title: Add them to the list
step.listExtend.text: Python takes the top plate off and adds each of its object’s items to the list further down the plates.

step.copy.subject: step
step.copy.title: Copy a label
step.copy.text: Python makes a second label for an object already on the plates, and puts it on top.

step.swap.subject: step
step.swap.title: Swap two plates
step.swap.text: Python swaps the top plate with one further down, so the next steps find them in the order they need.

step.unpackSequence.subject: step
step.unpackSequence.title: Unpack into {count}
step.unpackSequence.text: Python takes the object off the top plate and puts each of its {count} on a plate of its own, ready to be stored.

step.yieldValue.subject: step
step.yieldValue.title: Hand back an item, and pause
step.yieldValue.text: The generator takes the label off the top plate and hands it to whoever asked for the next item. Its frame waits, with its plates as they are, until it is asked again.

step.returnGenerator.subject: step
step.returnGenerator.title: Make a generator
step.returnGenerator.text: A function with yield in it doesn’t run straight away. This step makes a generator object, which runs the function’s steps one item at a time, when asked.

step.raiseVarargs.subject: step
step.raiseVarargs.title: Raise an error
step.raiseVarargs.text: Python takes the error off the top plate and raises it. Python stops running the steps in order, and looks for code that handles the error.

step.pushExcInfo.subject: step
step.pushExcInfo.title: Catch the error
step.pushExcInfo.text: The error is caught. Python puts it on a plate, ready for the steps that handle it.

step.checkExcMatch.subject: step
step.checkExcMatch.title: Is it this kind of error?
step.checkExcMatch.text: Python checks whether the error on the plates is the kind this **except** names, and puts the answer, True or False, on a plate.

step.popExcept.subject: step
step.popExcept.title: Done with the error
step.popExcept.text: The error has been handled. Python takes it off its plate and goes back to the error it was handling before, if any.

step.reraise.subject: step
step.reraise.title: Raise the error again
step.reraise.text: Python raises the error on the top plate again, for code further out to handle.

step.importName.subject: step
step.importName.title: Import {name}
step.importName.text: Python finds the module **{name}**, running its code the first time, and puts a label for the module on a plate.

step.importFrom.subject: step
step.importFrom.title: Get {name} from the module
step.importFrom.text: Python looks up **{name}** in the module on the top plate and puts a label for it on a plate.

step.nop.subject: step
step.nop.title: Do nothing
step.nop.text: A step that does nothing. The compiler leaves it where a line of your program needs no step of its own, so tools can still see the line.

step.other.subject: step
step.other.title: A {opname} step
step.other.text: Python has many kinds of step. This one, **{opname}**, doesn’t have its own explanation here yet.

tryIt.disRow.lines.subject: program
tryIt.disRow.lines.text: The line of your file each group of steps comes from. 0 is Python’s own setup step, before line 1.

tryIt.disRow.linesNoSetup.subject: program
tryIt.disRow.linesNoSetup.text: The line of your file each group of steps comes from.

tryIt.disRow.labels.subject: program
tryIt.disRow.labels.text: Labels for places the steps jump to. A step that jumps names the label it jumps to.

tryIt.disRow.code.subject: step
tryIt.disRow.code.text: {code}’s own steps. The number after **at** is where its code object sat in memory; it changes every time you run it.

tryIt.disRow.loadGlobalNull.subject: step
tryIt.disRow.loadGlobalNull.text: Find **{name}**, and add an empty plate. The number holds both: which name, counting from 0, doubled, plus 1 for “add the empty plate”.

tryIt.disRow.loadFast.subject: step
tryIt.disRow.loadFast.text: {code}’s own variable **{name}**: the number says which, counting from 0.

tryIt.disRow.loadConst.subject: step
tryIt.disRow.loadConst.text: A fixed value from the recipe card: the number says which, counting from 0, and dis shows it in brackets.

tryIt.level6.links.subject: program
tryIt.level6.links.text: The C on this zoom level, on GitHub at CPython’s v3.14.2 tag. These links open GitHub, outside this app:

tryIt.adaptiveRow.subject: step
tryIt.adaptiveRow.text: Step {number} of {code}: {opname} before the run, this form after it.

1.intro: Save your program in a file called {file}, open a [[terminal|terminal]] in the same folder, and type:

parts.text: Start Python. On Windows you can also type py.
The file for Python to run.

read: Type your program exactly as it is here, with the same spaces, and press Enter after the last line before you save. Then your file holds the same {bytes} that zoom level 2 shows.

2.intro: Ask Python to show the numbers stored in your file:

parts.text: Run the small piece of Python inside the quotes, without making a new file.
Open your file. **r** means read it, **b** means as raw bytes, not as text.
Turn the bytes into a list of ordinary numbers.

read: Some Windows editors end each line with two bytes, 13 then 10. If yours does, your list has a 13 before every 10.

3.intro: Ask Python’s tokenizer to list the tokens it finds in your file:

parts.text: Run **tokenize**, the tokenizer that comes with Python, as a program.

4.intro: Ask Python to print the structure of your file as text:

parts.text: Run **ast**, Python’s module for the structure of code, as a program.

5.intro: Ask Python to show the bytecode it made from your file:

parts.text: Run **dis**, which shows bytecode in a readable form. The name is short for “disassemble”.

read: dis shows the steps as the compiler made them, before the program runs. It doesn’t show how Python rewrites them while it runs.

6.command: python -c "import dis; c = compile(open('{file}').read(), '{file}', 'exec'); exec(c, dict(__name__='__main__')); dis.dis(c, adaptive=True)"
6.intro: Run your file, then ask Python which forms its steps had become:

parts.text: Load **dis**, which shows bytecode in a readable form.
Read your file and compile it into bytecode, as python {file} does.
Run it, as your program itself. While it runs, Python rewrites steps into faster forms.
Show the steps as they are now: **adaptive=True** asks for the forms Python rewrote them into.

read: First comes what your program printed. Then the steps, as python -m dis shows them at the zoom level before this one, but in the forms they had become.
Python rewrites some steps the first time they run, and others only once they have run a few times. A step that never ran keeps its general form.
